content: 1. Infected individuals will be provided with health-protection advice to prevent the progression of the disease and reduce the risk of transmission. 2. Efforts will be made to increase the initiation of hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, improve treatment completion rates, and enhance sustained virologic response (SVR). 3. There is a risk of stigmatization associated with identifying individuals with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and/or HCV infections. 4. In areas where poverty is prevalent and access to healthcare services is limited, incentivizing individuals to seek hepatitis care may pose a significant challenge. 5. Few studies have been conducted on quality improvement initiatives or integration strategies for HBV care. 6. Counseling is a recognized standard in HIV testing services and is essential for supporting adherence. However, counseling for hepatitis testing services has not been well-established. 7. Simple educational interventions for lay healthcare workers require minimal training, incur low costs, are highly feasible, and can significantly scale up HBV screening. 8. Healthcare workers (HCWs) must understand the strengths and limitations of counseling patients who undergo screening. 9. HCWs should be aware of the importance of reminders to enhance hepatitis screening during medical consultations. 10. Coordinated mental health and substance abuse services within HCV care delivery will require new training and systems. However, linking these services to HCV treatment initiation, improving treatment completion, and increasing SVR will enhance cure rates and prevent further HCV transmission. 11. Increasing hepatitis B and C screening rates will improve equity in access to care and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. 12. No major ethical concerns are associated with these recommendations. 13. Establishing proper patient databases to record clinician reminders for HCV testing may be costly. However, no additional costs are required to expand facility-based HCV screening in settings with electronic records or analogous reminder systems. 14. Coordinated mental health and substance abuse services within HCV care delivery will require stakeholder involvement. 15. These recommendations will increase opportunities for hepatitis screening and are relevant across various circumstances. 16. Linkages and referral pathways should be established for individuals infected with hepatitis viruses and those suffering from mental health problems. 17. Support from management and service providers is essential for successful implementation. 18. Scientific implementation research, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, is urgently needed to optimize chronic viral hepatitis service delivery systems. 19. Costing studies need to be conducted to better understand the financial implications of these interventions. 20. There is mounting evidence supporting the efficacy of antiviral therapy in reducing disease progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). 21. Despite fulfilling most criteria for systematic screening, HBV screening is not performed systematically due to factors such as lack of awareness, unclear guidelines, competing healthcare priorities, limited budgets, and insufficient political will. 22. Many individuals remain undiagnosed until the later stages of the disease, when prognosis is poor. Even when diagnosed, access to appropriate antiviral therapy and ongoing clinical management is often lacking. 23. For HBV screening in lowand middle-income countries, categorizing populations into high-risk groups is not particularly helpful or informative for guiding policy. 24. Screening programs should ensure that all members of the population have access, including through community outreach and healthcare facility-based screening. 25. The report serves as a summary of existing studies on the cost-effectiveness of HBV screening and treatment, with an analytic summary of key considerations. 26. There is a lack of relevant literature in lowand middle-income countries, so existing studies from high-income countries are described, with their potential uses and limitations discussed. 27. An updated search was conducted using PubMed to retrieve further relevant articles on HBV screening and treatment cost-effectiveness. 28. Older studies were excluded as they primarily focused on pre-vaccination screening rather than screening for antiviral therapy consideration. 29. Known ongoing HBV screening programs in lowand middle-income countries were included by consulting colleagues at the World Health Organization (WHO).
